title: 🍿 Comic Con shows what’s next for the entertainment industry
body_text: It happens to all of us: our team is getting smoked on national television. That happens to all of us, right? No matter, but maybe you just want to look away from the game where your quarterback can’t hit a pass for his life, the coach seems as perplexed as you are, and maybe you wince as Cam Skattebo continues to possess the self-preservation instincts of a lit firework. So, you look at your Instagram or something. Well, guess what: advertisers apparently saw that coming. Genius Sports , a UK-data company, has developed a complex map of 250 million American sports fans and collaborates with brands — food delivery companies are a particular favorite, as people tend to notice their own hunger when their team is not sufficiently distracting them — to serve up ads to fans of teams that are losing at especially distraction-prone moments. Apparently one of the major delivery companies sees a 20% uplift in prices when a fan’s team is losing. Stocks rose on Friday as the US struck a deal with Russia to release diesel to international markets helped ease crude prices. Last week saw a number of shifts in the entertainment industry, the largest of which was the long-sought merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. into Skydance , but also saw Netflix indicating that it was weighing layoffs , and Disney indicating it may directly take on Imax . At a glance, the fortunes of the entertainment sector appear to be shifting rapidly, with the future of it relatively cloudy. Last week, though, New York Comic Con offered insight into the future of the industry and intriguing clues as to why the entertainment properties that draw the most eyeballs are increasingly rarely coming from boardrooms in Los Angeles. Remember, entertainment companies are not structured to make money from new ideas. They are companies designed to extract continuous, multifaceted value from ideas they already own. Disney is the archetype of this. Making $12 from a movie ticket is nice, but once the customer is sufficiently entranced by the character, they make $30 from the Halloween costume, $20 from the doll sale, $10 a month from the Disney+ subscription to rewatch the movie, a thousand or more from the cruise and Disney World trip, $80 for the Broadway show ticket, and so on. Historically generating new ideas was done through internal R&D (like making a new movie or character) but lately these companies have been more content to acquire R&D from other, smaller shops. Disney buying Lucasfilm or Marvel fits this model. Amazon Prime’s two biggest shows, “The Boys” and “Invincible,” each raiding the independent press section of the comic shop is another. You can also see how the failure to make a property sufficiently exploitable can cause a problem. Take Netflix; on one hand, they certainly made some ancillary money from its demogorgon stuffies and Broadway show, but “Stranger Things” won’t be stuffing a lot of stockings this year despite the enormous IP investment. On the other hand, “KPop Demon Hunters,” which they bought off Sony, stands to be like every third Halloween costume this year. NYCC is illuminating because it shows the sources of original and speculative R&D on the rise, what’s resonating with audiences, and what’s going to sui generis pop , revealing which fast-growing franchises will be the next Marvel, the The Walking Dead, the next Romantasy to highlight three franchises that were big at NYCC well before becoming billion-dollar grossers for these large content exploitation companies. Dan Buckley, the publisher at Marvel, spoke candidly at the ICV2 Insider Talks panel about why comics have historically been of interest to these large companies: it is a relatively capital- un intensive business. Basically, you can make a comic and if it fails, no biggie. This same is true of books, manga, webtoons, really any situation where you’re paying one creator and shipping cheap pixels or dead trees. It’s not the case with a $200 million movie. If there was a star of this year’s NYCC, it’s likely “Dungeon Crawler Carl” scribe Dan Dinnamman , whose books have been a breakout hit of the emerging LitRPG genre; Comcast snagged the rights for that, which is developing a show for Peacock. For that matter, books, comics, and manga in general: per the ICV2 White Paper presentation, graphic novel sales are up 28% in the first half of 2026, and manga sales are up 39.5% in the book channel; it should not come as a surprise that Netflix (with “One Piece”) and Sony (through Crunchyroll) are pushing manga adaptations. Realistically, breakout IP hits are what define the long-term success of these megacompanies and will define their businesses for the coming years far more than any corporate structure. You make lots of cheap bets and one of them resonates with audiences at which point you can roll it into your lucrative (though capital-intensive) businesses, like cruises and theme parks. Sure, there is fear, uncertainty and doubt about the Warner-Paramount merger within the industry, but its success or failure will likely be defined less by how efficiently they can exploit existing IP — like the announced GI Joe and Transformers adaptations, which I’m certain will be incredibly culturally relevant when they eventually come out — but rather if they make savvy decisions about what new material to buy up. One deal in particular announced last week is intriguing for the future of where these companies are going to source the next generation of stories, and it’s not two dessicated cable companies casting their lots together. Marvel announced a few new projects to compete for new readers, including book publication formats that imitate the smash-hit DC Compact Comics, which in turn imitate the overwhelmingly popular manga book format. But the big one is that after years of unsuccessfully attempting to win over mobile phone-using audiences, Marvel has cut a deal with Webtoon , which dominates the category, to launch its Marvel Comics by Webtoon app . body_text: Airports aren’t exactly the most hassle-free havens on earth, with endless lines, regular delays, and ever-changing baggage regulations, but some are objectively more taxing than others. The bad news for frequent Dallas/Fort Worth flyers? Their airport of choice might just be the most stressful in the US, according to a new analysis from Rightway Parking . The online parking reservation site assessed American airports on five factors (delay rate, cancellation rate, how delays have worsened since 2021, and distance and travel time from downtown) and found the Texas travel hub to be the most stress-inducing, with O’Hare International not far behind. Stocks fell on Thursday as crude oil prices rose and chipmakers fell after the Financial Times reported that OpenAI’s revenue is around $20 billion less than previously indicated. Not only is the leader of the free world’s new artificial intelligence rebrand taking off with the world’s richest man, after Elon Musk announced he’d rename the SpaceX artificial intelligence division SpaceXSI last weekend, it’s also causing an explosion of registrations for the domain typically associated with sites in Slovenia. Like Anguilla before it, thanks to its .ai domain , the European nation of around 2.1 million people now finds itself with a small role in the unending conversation around artificial, or super, intelligence. A spokesperson for Registry.si — the organization responsible for providing domain registrations and ensuring online services under the Slovenian national domain run smoothly — told the BBC that the demand for .si addresses was “ unprecedented ” toward the end of September, after President Trump pressed ahead with the idea of switching the “A” out of “AI.” According to data from registration tracker Domain Name Stat, the Registry.si representative has a point. Over the last seven days, there have been some 63,000 new .si domain registrations, as hype around the idea of super intelligence spreads beyond Washington documents and billionaire boardrooms. To put that in perspective, there were just over 50,000 registrations from the start of 2024 to the beginning of 2026. It’s still too early to predict just how far “ the new world of super intelligence ,” as the president put it when he first posited the term at the UN General Assembly last month, will catch on as a term. However, if founders looking to pivot to “SI” or online entrepreneurs hoping to flip domains for profit keep buying up the .si addresses, the Slovenian government could enjoy a potential windfall, with Anguilla making at least ~$70 million from AI domain registrations last year, per our previous calculations . The biggest awards in television will no longer be on television from 2027 onward, after Amazon announced that it’s signed a six-year deal to make Prime Video the new and exclusive home of the annual Emmy awards. The company revealed that viewers will be able to stream the ceremony live without a subscription, in another sign that network television may no longer be the natural home for awards shows, after last year’s announcement that the Oscars will be moving to YouTube from 2029. With waning viewership and signs that online buzz around the Emmys might also be waning — YouTube search interest has roughly halved from its peak in 2013 —, quite why Amazon wants the once must-watch and now might-watch TV awards show isn’t all that clear. CEO Ramón Laguarta conceded “we don’t feel good about the beverage business” and that the company is putting “all the urgency” into improving its soda business. title: ⚛️ Argon or not
body_text: It’s rare to find an investment that pays off immediately and astronomically, but a treasure hunter scouring the Michigan estate sale of a local physician scored the jackpot: he bought a painting of several shells for $30 that was ultimately discovered to be “Alderman Merriam’s Shells,” a 1951 painting by Gertrude Abercrombie . The artist had traded the painting to the doctor in exchange for medical services. The painting just sold at auction for $1.3 million . Last week, Google’s DeepMind announced that it was releasing Gemini Argon 4 to a select group of testers, but it was the specs of the model and its performance on a battery of exams that really got people’s attention. That performance also has some significant relevance to investors, because if the benchmarks hold up, Google has managed to succeed in a number of areas where its competitors have ceded ground: While the major AI labs have all been churning out products on the frontier, amid all the chaos of new models — Opus 5.5! Fable! Astra! — the understanding of who commands the bleeding edge of AI development has actually been rather boring. Based on LMArena, it’s been Anthropic’s Claude dominating the rankings, and since March Claude has been a strong favorite on prediction markets to finish the year as the best AI. That’s why Argon is so interesting: even though it hasn’t been rolled out to customers, the performance of the model was so solid that, in the week since it was revealed, Gemini jumped neck-and-neck with Claude *. The details on Argon’s benchmarking posted by Demis Hassabis, Alphabet ’s top AI honcho, made it clear that it’s good at navigating dense legalese, is top of the line at business automation, and makes stuff up way less: Argon appears to have crushed the competition on Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark , coming in at a score of 19.6% compared to nearest runner-up Claude Fable’s 6.7%. Also of note is the performance on AutomationBench , a benchmark from Zapier about how good models are at basic daily tasks in sales (such as lead management, CRM), marketing (ad performance), finance (expenses and bookkeeping) and HR (payroll and onboarding). There, it outran the nearest competition by nearly ten points. Those analyzing the model’s performance have also found something else impressive: Argon also appears to have knocked it out of the park when it comes to reining in hallucinations. According to the AA-Omniscience Hallucination Rate , which calculates how often a model answers incorrectly when it gives a partial or non-response, is the lowest on the frontier, at just 15%. That’s obviously not zero, but a major improvement compared to GPT-6 Astra (45%) and Opus 5.5 (59%). This doesn’t mean you can replace your lawyer with Argon, but… if you are a company that earns a solid slice of billable hours consulting, offering basic legal advice, human resource services, or actionable intelligence, I might be a little worried about the AI in every client’s email getting sharper at precisely these tasks. These developments might be especially relevant for Google’s business in particular. Several of their peers in AI development have understandably focused their efforts on designing models that are particularly good at coding . From a long-term ROI perspective, it makes sense for technology companies to invest in tools that can build better tools . There’s also tons of online material about how to code for AI to ingest. And of course, humans who develop software are just incredibly expensive, and if you can build a robot that develops software you can sell it to a lot of fabulously wealthy technology companies and make a lot of money before you IPO. While some of those incentives are advantageous for Alphabet, the more important element here is to think about what makes Alphabet’s core customer more unique. Nevermind coders, Alphabet has lots and lots of corporate G Suite customers and even more people who just use elements of the Google family of products. How Google will make money from AI is by creating tools that can be used by the companies and people that already pay Google. In other words, Alphabet’s best shot at dominating an AI niche is to build within the business services niche it already dominates, selling to the hundreds of millions of people who work non-software jobs who want useful tools for those jobs. That’s why the Argon result is just so eye-popping, and why the rollout of Argon could be a make-or-break moment not just for Alphabet, but for the scores of companies that Argon may very well disrupt. Just ask the software developers and SaaS companies how fun it was for them when Claude would demonstrate on a weekly basis how delicious it found their lunch to be.
